title: Twenty thousand rows a second
subtitle: A batch update that took twenty-five seconds became a third of a second: one SQL rewrite that makes parameter count independent of row count, and nearly 400 GB of indexes that nobody had ever read

stats.label: per batch update, down from 25 s, with more rows in each
rows per second, up from 50, read from the database's own counters
per row at most after the rewrite, and as low as 0.06 ms

lede: My research pipeline writes its results back to PostgreSQL through one governed write path, and in a 3.4-million-item run that path was the bottleneck. Each batch update of about 1,350 rows cost roughly 19 milliseconds a row, and the queue behind it grew past 140,000 messages. Two changes fixed it: a different shape of UPDATE statement, and the removal of indexes that had never been used. The original update built a table of values inline, joined it to the target and bound one parameter per cell. PostgreSQL allows 65,535 bind parameters per statement, so a twenty-column payload capped a batch at a few thousand rows, and the planner materialised the whole derived table before it could join.
quote: A queue message is not a row.
evidence: PostgreSQL performance tuning: a batch update cut from 25 s to 0.3 s by binding one array per column, with per-row cost of 0.06-0.19 ms.
SQL query design: a parameter count independent of row count under PostgreSQL's 65,535 bind-parameter limit, with the old form kept as a fallback.
Index cost analysis: never-scanned approximate-nearest-neighbour indexes found through two catalog queries and dropped, with recreation commands kept for rollback.
Throughput measurement methodology: throughput read from the database's own tuple and commit counters, 50 to 20,000 rows per second, never from queue length.
author: Corey James
